title: Inverting a Binary Tree

phrases.phrase: swap the left and right children
phrases.explanation: Exchange the left child node and the right child node of a given node
Visit every node in the tree in a systematic order
The simplest condition in a recursive function where no further recursion is needed
A reflection of the original structure, flipped horizontally
Processing nodes one depth at a time, from top to bottom

technical_terms.definition: A tree data structure where each node has at most two children, called left and right
A technique where a function calls itself to solve smaller subproblems
Breadth-First Search, a traversal that visits all nodes at the current depth before moving deeper
Depth-First Search, a traversal that explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking
A first-in, first-out data structure used to process elements in order

java_methods.description: Creates a new queue backed by a linked list, commonly used for BFS traversal
Adds a node to the end of the queue

concept: Given the root of a binary tree, invert the tree by swapping the left and right children at every node, and return the root of the inverted tree.

solutions.label: Recursive DFS
solutions.summary: Use recursion to visit every node depth-first and swap its left and right children.

solutions.label: Iterative BFS
solutions.summary: Use a queue to traverse the tree level by level, swapping children at each node.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here's your problem. You're given the root of a binary tree. I want you to invert the entire tree. By invert, I mean swap the left and right children of every single node, so the result is a mirror image of the original.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. So just to clarify, each node can have at most two children, and I need to swap left and right at every node, not just the root. What should I return?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Return the root of the inverted tree. The tree nodes have an integer value, a left pointer, and a right pointer. The tree could be empty, meaning the root is null.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: What about edge cases? If the tree is null, I return null. If there's only one node with no children, I just return that node as is, right?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Exactly. Both of those should be handled. Let's use this example: root is four, left child is two, right child is seven. Node two has children one and three. After inverting, seven moves to the left, two moves to the right, and two's children also swap.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Understood. So the output tree has four at the root, seven on the left, two on the right, and under two, three is on the left and one is on the right. Let me think about approaches.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: My first idea is a recursive approach. For each node, I recursively invert the left subtree, then the right subtree, and then swap the two children. The base case is when the node is null, I just return null.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Walk me through the example with that approach.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Starting at node four, I go left to node two. At node two, I go left to one, which has no children, so I return it. Then I go right to three, also no children. Now I swap one and three under node two. Back at four, I visit seven, which is a leaf. Finally I swap two and seven under four. Done.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What about time and space complexity?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Time is O of n because we visit every node once. Space is O of h where h is the height of the tree, due to the recursion call stack. In the worst case of a skewed tree, that's O of n. For a balanced tree, it's O of log n.

sections.title: Iterative BFS Approach
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    style A fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style B fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style C fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style D fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style E fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    subgraph "Queue Processing"
    Q1["Queue: [4]"] --> Q2["Swap 4's children → Queue: [7, 2]"]
    Q2 --> Q3["Swap 7's children (none) → Queue: [2]"]
    Q3 --> Q4["Swap 2's children → Queue: [3, 1]"]
    Q4 --> Q5["Process leaves → Queue empty"]
    end
    subgraph Result
    A((4)) --> B((7))
    A --> C((2))
    C --> D((3))
    C --> E((1))
    end

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: An alternative is an iterative solution using BFS. I use a queue starting with the root. For each node I dequeue, I swap its left and right children, then add both children to the queue if they're not null.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Can you trace through the same example?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Sure. Queue starts with four. I dequeue four and swap its children, so now seven is left and two is right. I enqueue seven and two. Next I dequeue seven, it has no children to swap. Then I dequeue two, swap its children one and three. I enqueue three and one. Both are leaves, so nothing to swap. Queue is empty, we're done.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: And the complexity for this approach?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Time is still O of n since we process every node. Space is O of n in the worst case because the queue could hold up to n over two nodes at the widest level of the tree. This avoids recursion, so there's no risk of stack overflow on deep trees.

sections.title: Summary
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    subgraph Comparison
    A["Recursive DFS\nTime: O of n\nSpace: O of h"] --- B["Iterative BFS\nTime: O of n\nSpace: O of n"]
    end
    style A fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style B fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Good work. Can you summarize the two approaches?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Both run in O of n time. The recursive DFS is the cleanest solution, just three lines of logic, and uses O of h space on the call stack. The iterative BFS uses a queue and takes O of n space, but it avoids recursion which can be important for very deep trees. For an interview, I'd go with the recursive approach for its simplicity.
